title: Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps

epigraph.quote: It's far better to buy a wonderful company at a fair price than a fair company at a wonderful price.
epigraph.author: Warren Buffett, Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letter, 1989

web_blocks.text: Greaves Cotton closed at ₹225.97 on Friday 13 November 2026, up 1.25% on the day and 11.11% on the week [108]. One dating point first. The TradingView snapshot was taken after the NSE close on 13 November, but our facts ledger still held the 12 November bar of ₹223.18 for this stock, as it did for 535 of the 543 names it tracks [118]. The gap is one trading day, and every level here uses ₹225.97. Market capitalisation is price times shares: ₹225.97 × 23.2951 crore shares is about ₹5,264 crore, matching Screener [109]. TradingView lists ₹5,199 crore because it applies its own share count, so the peer table below shows that lower figure for Greaves.

Chapter 1 held back the price record so the business could be read without it. By fiscal year (April to March) and from unadjusted monthly closes, it shows three cycles [111]. The engine-led cycle of FY15-FY19 peaked at ₹178.6 in FY18. Covid then took the stock to about ₹66 near March 2020, roughly 63% lower. The 2021-22 rally reached ₹258.9, nearly four times the low, and by FY23 the stock was 54% below it. FY25 set the record high of ₹319.5, and FY26 bottomed at ₹120.0, about 62% lower. Today's price is 16.9% below the FY27 high of ₹271.9 and 88% above the 52-week low of ₹119.99 [108][118].

web_blocks.caption: Share price by fiscal year (₹; unadjusted monthly closes; FY27 to 13 November 2026) beside the business at the time
rows: BS-VI and Covid; low near ₹66 in March 2020 [12]
EBITDA ₹80 crore, net loss, yet price recovering [11]

web_blocks.takeaway: The two peaks that followed the weakest earnings, FY22 and FY25, were paid for the electric story and later given back, while the engine-earnings years of FY17 and FY18 moved within a high-to-low range of about ₹62 to ₹66, far narrower than the swings around the FY22 and FY25 peaks. The price has often led or ignored current profit, then repriced when cash failed to appear.

web_blocks.text: Price and earnings parted company three times. In FY21 the shares doubled off the low while EBITDA fell to ₹80 crore. In FY22 they hit ₹258.9 at a 1.5% group margin. In FY25 they hit ₹319.5 at 4.7%. Our reading is that investors paid for the electric subsidiary's growth story, then marked it down as FAME-II losses, negative operating cash flow and rising borrowings appeared [6][60]. Today's price is 29.3% below the FY25 peak although FY26 EBITDA of ₹239 crore is the best since FY19. Patience has been poorly paid: from the March 2017 close of ₹171.1 the gain is about 3% a year before dividends (our calculation [118]), while trailing EBITDA moved only from ₹240 crore to ₹260 crore [60][109].

web_blocks.caption: What the ₹225.97 is made of (₹ crore unless stated)
rows: Market cap − (cash and investments 606 − borrowings 513) + leases 55, September 2026; GEML's 37.5% minority not added [1][2][118]
EV / TTM EBITDA; EV / TTM sales
EBITDA includes GEML's −₹63 crore in H1 FY27 [1][118]
web_blocks.takeaway: Enterprise value, equity value plus debt less cash, is almost the same as market cap here because cash and borrowings roughly offset. The offset is weaker than it looks, since part of the cash sits inside the loss-making subsidiary and part of the debt funds the EV lender's loan book [6][97].

web_blocks.text: Do not read the 58-67x trailing P/E as a clean signal. Trailing profit is depressed by GEML's EBITDA loss of ₹63 crore in H1 FY27 and ₹60.1 crore of one-offs in Q2 [1][2]. At 58.2x the implied profit is only about ₹90 crore (our calculation [118]), against ₹107.14 crore attributable to shareholders in FY26 [6]. A high ratio on a damaged number says the market is looking past current earnings, which the next sections test. On our FY28 base-case owner earnings of about ₹9.1 a share, the same price is 24.8x, a forecast and not a fact [118].

web_blocks.the_number: At ₹225.97 the market is pricing about 12.5% revenue growth a year for ten years from ₹4,026 crore, if group EBITDA margin rises from 6.5% to 12% by year five and holds. Year-ten revenue would be about ₹13,070 crore, 3.2 times today's. A reverse DCF takes the price as given and solves for the growth and margin that make discounted future cash flows equal it.
web_blocks.how_calculated: We forecast ten years of free cash flow, add a terminal value, discount at 12.5% and solve for the growth that equates the total to enterprise value of ₹5,226 crore. The margin ramps in a straight line over five years. WACC, the weighted average cost of capital, is the return investors need from the whole business.
web_blocks.the_inputs: EV ₹5,226 crore, TTM revenue ₹4,026 crore, TTM EBITDA ₹260 crore [109][118]. Our assumptions: WACC 12.5%, terminal growth 5.5%, tax 25%, depreciation 3.0% and capex 3.5% of revenue, working capital 10% of added revenue [118].
web_blocks.the_range: Growth needed is 24.1% at an 8% margin, 17.0% at 10%, 12.5% at 12% and 9.3% at 14%. For reference, group revenue grew 28% trailing, core revenue 20% in H1 FY27, and the FY15-FY26 record is about 6.6% a year [1][60].
web_blocks.if_off: The bar is slightly understated because GEML's minority is not in EV. If the true year-five margin is 10%, the price needs about 17% growth for a decade, above anything Greaves has sustained.

web_blocks.caption: Reverse DCF sensitivities over ten years (our calculation [118])
web_blocks.takeaway: A higher margin lets the same price be justified with less growth, and the reverse also holds. Management's guidance sits between the rows, which is why the price is neither obviously cheap nor out of reach, but the group has not earned 12% since FY19 [60][28].

web_blocks.text: We go slightly beyond the first-pass reading. A simple story says the price is fair if the core holds about 12% and GEML breaks even. Test it on our FY28 base case: core revenue of about ₹3,616 crore at 13.5% earns ₹488 crore, GEML revenue of ₹1,872 crore earns nothing, and the group margin is about 8.9% (our calculation [118]). The table says 9% needs 20% growth for ten years. To reach 12% at that mix, GEML would need a margin of about 9%, when Ather runs at about −6.9% [116]. So the price needs one part of the business to surprise. It credits the core with a recovery and gives GEML the benefit of the doubt.

A sum-of-the-parts valuation (SOTP) values each business at the multiple it deserves and adds them. The core earned ₹383 crore of EBITDA at 14.4% in FY26, so EV/EBITDA (enterprise value over operating profit) fits it [4]. GEML has never earned an operating profit, so only EV/Sales works. With GEML at zero and Greaves Finance at ₹150 crore, the market pays about 13.3x FY26 core EBITDA, or 10.4x our FY28 base of ₹488 crore (our calculation [118]).

web_blocks.caption: SOTP scenarios on FY28E (year to March 2028), valued at November 2028 (our judgment inputs; core FY26 revenue ₹2,665 crore)
web_blocks.takeaway: Core margin and core multiple do almost all the work. Core is 90% of base equity value and GEML 7%, so the stock is mainly a valuation of the engine and genset core, with GEML an option that costs ₹150 crore of leakage in the bear case if another funding round comes [118].

web_blocks.the_number: ₹288.7 a share is our probability-weighted value at November 2028: 27.8% above ₹225.97, about 13.0% a year over 24 months, and 38.7% above the ₹208.14 support, about 17.8% a year. Our base-case target is ₹303.
web_blocks.how_calculated: 25% × ₹427 + 45% × ₹303 + 30% × ₹152. Each scenario is core EBITDA × multiple, plus 62.5% of GEML revenue × EV/Sales, plus Greaves Finance at ₹150 crore and ₹38 crore of net cash, less bear-case leakage, over 23.2951 crore shares.
web_blocks.the_inputs: Core FY26 revenue ₹2,665 crore [4][118]; paths that bracket 16-20% growth and 13-15% margin guidance [28][1]; Sep-2026 cash ₹606 crore, borrowings ₹513 crore, leases ₹55 crore [2]. Probabilities, multiples and GEML EV/Sales are our judgments. A 30x cross-check on FY28E owner earnings of about ₹9.1 gives ₹273 [118].
web_blocks.the_range: Bull ₹427, base ₹303, bear ₹152, still above the 52-week low of ₹119.99. Peers trade at trailing P/Es of 48-56x (Kirloskar 47.9x, Cummins 53.8x, TVS 55.8x), so 30x forward is a discount for weaker returns, though trailing against forward is a loose match [112][113][114].
web_blocks.if_off: Each 1x of core multiple moves the base by about ₹21 and each point of core margin by about ₹20. At today's 12.0% margin and 13x the base is about ₹273, and at 11% about ₹253, returns near 10% and 6% a year from ₹225.97, below a 12% hurdle [118].

web_blocks.caption: How the base value moves if core margin stays near today's level or the multiple falls (₹ per share; our calculation [118])
rows: Needs the full recovery from today's 12.0%
No recovery: management has said progress is slower than planned
web_blocks.takeaway: Holding the core margin at its H1 FY27 level of 12.0% takes the base value from ₹303 to about ₹273, and a lower 11x multiple takes it to about ₹236, so margin recovery is the hinge of the valuation. Each cell keeps the other base inputs unchanged: core revenue of ₹3,616 crore, GEML at 0.45x sales, Greaves Finance at ₹150 crore and a ₹38 crore net cash adjustment [1][118].

web_blocks.caption: Peer snapshot, 13 November 2026 (TradingView; trailing figures as provided; Greaves added for reference)
web_blocks.takeaway: Greaves earns the lowest return of the profitable group yet trades above all of them on trailing P/E, because its earnings are depressed and its story is electric [112][113][114][115][116]. Read the margin column with care: it is TradingView's operating margin after depreciation, trailing twelve months, which is about 3.1% for Greaves. The 6.5% group figure used elsewhere in this report is EBITDA margin, before depreciation of about ₹137 crore, so the two do not conflict [109][118].

web_blocks.text: Kirloskar Oil Engines and Cummins India, the direct comparisons for Energy Solutions, are both in Weinstein Stage 4, a downtrend, down about 18% in three months [112][113]. They earn ROCE of 14.6% and 39.5% against Greaves's 10.1% [112][113][109]. The engine group is being de-rated while Greaves has been re-rated, which points to the electric story. It does not prove mispricing, because Kirloskar's Q2 FY27 margin squeeze (14.0% to 11.0%) is the same commodity lag Greaves faced [81].

TVS Motor shows what a profitable petrol business can fund, with a 55.8x P/E, 12.5% operating margin and a 26.28% share of January-October e2W registrations [114][85]. Ola Electric is the failure base rate: revenue −49% and operating margin −94%, yet a market value of ₹17,860 crore, so a market value is not a floor [115]. Ather, at ₹76,242 crore on a −6.9% operating margin, shows what investors pay for scale [116]. That is about ₹25.9 lakh per registration (2,94,127 in January-October) against about ₹1 lakh for GEML at our base value of ₹842 crore at 100%, a gap of roughly 25 times [85][118]. The gap does not make Greaves cheap, since Ather is a premium brand with positive EBITDA. It shows the optionality in our bull case.

web_blocks.title: The weakest assumption, and what would falsify it
paragraphs: The weakest assumption is a base-case core margin of 13.5% by FY28E at 13x. H1 FY27 delivered 12.0%, management said margin improvement was “slower than we had anticipated”, and customer repricing lags metal costs by four to five months [24][62]. At 12.0% the base falls to about ₹273.

Core margin below 12% in Q3 FY27 (results around February 2027) and again in Q4 would shift weight to the bear case. A core margin of 13% or more, no further GEML funding round and positive operating cash flow would confirm it, and they are the conditions for our upgrade review in Chapter 9 [24].

web_blocks.text: The price is neither a free lunch nor a trap. Whether to act depends on where it sits inside its own structure, which Chapter 8 reads.

book_paragraphs: On Friday evening, 13 November 2026, a single number sat on the screen: ₹225.97. It looked solid, the way a price always does. But a price is a vote, not a fact, and the useful question is what the voters believe. So let us take the number apart and see what is inside it.

Start with the history, which we deliberately held back until now. If you plotted Greaves Cotton's shares since FY15 you would see three humps. The first, up to about ₹179 in FY18, belonged to the engine business, when the company earned 14 to 15 paise of operating profit on every rupee of sales and carried almost no debt. Then Covid arrived and the shares fell about 63% to nearly ₹66. The second hump, in FY22, took the price to ₹258.9, nearly four times that low. Here is the odd part. In that same year the group's operating margin was 1.5% and its operating cash flow was negative. The market was not paying for what the company earned. It was paying for the electric story.

The third hump is the most instructive. In FY25 the shares touched ₹319.5, the highest price in the whole record, and also ₹112.1 in the same twelve months. By FY26 they were back at ₹120. That is a fall of roughly 62% from the peak. Meanwhile the business was recovering: FY26 operating profit of ₹239 crore was its best since FY19. So the market had marked down the story faster than it had marked up the earnings. A patient holder from March 2017 would be sitting on a gain of about 32% over almost ten years, roughly 3% a year before dividends. Revenue had more than doubled. Profit had barely moved. What does that tell you? That growth is not worth what you pay for it unless it turns into cash.

Now look at what the price is made of. Multiply ₹225.97 by 23.2951 crore shares and you get a market value of about ₹5,264 crore. Subtract the cash, add the debt and the leases, and you get an enterprise value of ₹5,226 crore, which is roughly what a buyer would pay for the operating business. On trailing numbers that is about 20 times operating profit. The accounting hides two catches. Some of the cash sits inside the electric subsidiary after its ₹530 crore rights issue, and some of the debt is simply the lending arm's borrowing, matched against loans it has made.

You will also see that the share trades at 58 to 67 times trailing earnings, depending on whom you ask. Do not be alarmed, and do not be comforted. Trailing profit is small because the subsidiary lost ₹63 crore at the operating line in six months and because ₹60 crore of write-downs landed in one quarter. A high ratio on a small, damaged number tells you the market is looking through the damage. It does not tell you whether it is right to.

That is why we run a reverse DCF. Think of a restaurant bill. If someone tells you the bill was ₹5,226 crore, you can ask what the evening must have been like to justify it. A reverse DCF does the same with a share price. It asks what growth and what profit margin the business would need for ten years to be worth exactly today's price. The answer is about 12.5% revenue growth a year, as long as the group margin climbs from 6.5% to 12% by year five. Lower the margin to 10% and the growth needed jumps to 17%. At 8% it jumps to 24%. Greaves has grown revenue about 6.6% a year over eleven years.

Here we part company slightly with the easy story, which says the price is fair if the core holds its margin and the electric business merely breaks even. Do the sums on our own forecast and you find that a core earning 13.5% together with a breakeven subsidiary gives a group margin of about 8.9%, which needs growth of around 20% a year for a decade. To reach 12% the subsidiary would have to earn about 9%, and the only listed scooter maker that has come close to profit, Ather, still runs at a loss on its operating line. So the price needs a good outcome, not a miracle, and it needs one part of the business to surprise.

To value the two halves fairly we use a sum of the parts. Picture two shops under one roof. One is an old, profitable engine shop, which you value on its profit. The other is a young scooter shop with no profit yet, which you can only value on its sales. We built three scenarios for November 2028. In the bull case the engine shop earns 14.5% and gets a 16 times multiple, giving ₹427. In the base case it earns 13.5% at 13 times, giving ₹303. In the bear case the margin squeeze persists, the multiple falls to 9.5, and the scooter shop needs another ₹150 crore from its owners, giving ₹152. Weight those at 25%, 45% and 30% and you get ₹288.7, which is 27.8% above today's price, or about 13% a year.

Notice that even in the bull case the scooter shop supplies only a tenth of the value. When the CFO says, “We do not expect further funding for the next 12 to 18 months period at all and thereafter we expect the business generate cash on its own,” he is making a promise that matters more for the bear case than the bull one. When the CEO admits that “the improvement in margins has been slower than we had anticipated,” he is talking about the engine shop's margin, which is where the value is.

Peers help but they can mislead. The two big engine makers, Kirloskar and Cummins, are both in downtrends, down about 18% in three months, even though they earn better returns than Greaves. So the engine group is being marked down while Greaves is being marked up, and that is the electric story again. TVS shows what a profitable petrol business can fund. Ola shows how a pure-play can lose half its revenue and still hold a ₹17,860 crore market value. Ather, worth ₹76,242 crore, shows what the market will pay for scale: about twenty-five times more per scooter registered than our base case pays for Greaves's Ampere. That does not make Greaves cheap. It shows how much is possible if the scale arrives.

Benjamin Graham's old line says the market is a voting machine in the short run and a weighing machine in the long run. Today the vote is warm. The weighing will come in February 2027, when the Q3 numbers show whether the core margin is back at 13% or still stuck near 12%. If it is 12%, our base case drops to about ₹273 and the return from here is under 10% a year. If it is 11%, we are near ₹253 and the return falls to about 6%. That one number is the assumption we trust least, so it is the one to watch.

So what should you take from all this? The price is not a bargain at ₹225.97. A weighted return of about 13% a year only just clears a 12% hurdle, and the margin of safety is thin. But from the ₹205 to ₹211 area it would be about 18% a year, a very different bet. Price and value are two different things, and the gap between them is where we get paid. The next chapter asks whether the chart will let us wait for that gap.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: A share price is the market's current answer to a question about the future. Greaves has been asked that question three times, and twice the answer was too high and was withdrawn. The discipline is to ask what the price needs to be true, then to wait until you are paid for the risk that it is not.

web_title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps
question: What is today's price assuming, and how does it compare with peers?
